\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction across four models (1.5B--13B, three architecture families).
Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four models (${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds; 3-seed mean 96.58\% due to format collapse on one seed), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows 9.16pp scale sensitivity (67.3--76.5\%).
Adding more trace information provides no additional benefit: training dynamics show \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence.
The gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$74\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%) on Qwen-7B (single seed).
A format-marker ablation shows ${\sim}$91\% of the exception signal is semantic rather than format-driven, and cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench confirms generalization (\texttt{exception\_only}: 100\%, $N{=}426$).

The broader implication is that verdict prediction is not an information-starved task that benefits from richer context.
It is a fault detection task where the runtime has already surfaced the critical diagnostic signal; the model's role is to interpret whether that signal indicates a terminal fault (as the SFT advantage over regex on caught-exception cases confirms).
This reframing suggests a design principle for trace-augmented systems: extract the highest-specificity diagnostic signal (median 150 tokens) and discard everything else.
Our findings are established on LLM-generated Python code with exception-dominated error distributions; whether they hold for other languages, larger real-world codebases, production fault distributions with a higher proportion of silent logic errors (where no exception is raised), or tasks beyond verdict prediction remains an open question.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}
TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility to be task- and format-dependent, a finding we extend by identifying exception events as the dominant signal for verdict prediction.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} leveraged trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning.
\citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, supporting our information density finding.
\citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution traces for code understanding, and \citet{chen2024selfdebug} demonstrated that LLMs can self-debug by reasoning over execution results.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} established execution reasoning benchmarks, extended to 19 languages by \citet{xu2025cruxevalx}.
None decompose which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.

\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical analysis with deep learning.
In patch correctness, \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness} and CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec} pioneered representation learning of code changes; LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} reached 84.4\% using traces; APPT \citep{appt2024} achieved 79.7\%.
Test oracle generation progressed from ATLAS \citep{watson2020atlas} through retrieval-augmented approaches \citep{yu2022assertion,nashid2023assertion} to TOGA \citep{dinella2022toga}; FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated structured fault signals.
These approaches treat traces as monolithic inputs; none isolate individual components or compare against rule-based baselines.

\paragraph{Fault Localization.}
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra; classic metrics (Ochiai \citep{abreu2007accuracy}, Tarantula \citep{jones2002visualization}, DStar \citep{wong2014dstar}) and recent LLM-based approaches \citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl,widyasari2024llm4fl,mukherjee2025llmfl} share our core insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.
Verdict prediction is a prerequisite to FL: one must determine \emph{whether} a fault exists before localizing \emph{where}.
Our approach and SBFL operate at different granularities (test-level vs.\ statement-level) but exploit the same signal type.

\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}
TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction for debugging; RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent} and Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless} incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows.
\citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit, supporting our compression finding.
SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench} provides a realistic benchmark for agents reasoning about test execution.
Our approximate information density decomposition (gradient dilution ${\sim}$26\% vs.\ information overload ${\sim}$74\%) provides the first quantitative framework for \emph{why} compression helps, complementing these methods' focus on \emph{how} to compress.

\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}
Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,spiess2025calibration}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 suggests compact inputs improve calibration.
Just-in-time defect prediction progressed from feature engineering \citep{kamei2013large} through deep learning \citep{hoang2019deepjit} to simpler-but-effective approaches \citep{pornprasit2021jitline}; these methods share our fault detection motivation but operate on code change features rather than execution traces.

\paragraph{Training Efficiency and Data Selection.}
Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} show that data quality and ordering improve convergence, consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable rapid convergence while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}
TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility to be task- and format-dependent, a finding we extend by identifying exception events as the dominant signal for verdict prediction.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} leveraged trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning.
\citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, supporting our information density finding.
\citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution traces for code understanding, and \citet{chen2024selfdebug} demonstrated that LLMs can self-debug by reasoning over execution results.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} established execution reasoning benchmarks, extended to 19 languages by \citet{xu2025cruxevalx}.
None decompose which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy.

\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; DeepDFA \citep{steenhoek2024deepdfa} and learned program slicing \citep{yadavally2024slicing} combined classical analysis with deep learning.
In patch correctness, \citet{tian2020patchcorrectness} and CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec} pioneered representation learning of code changes; LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} reached 84.4\% using traces; APPT \citep{appt2024} achieved 79.7\%.
Test oracle generation progressed from ATLAS \citep{watson2020atlas} through retrieval-augmented approaches \citep{yu2022assertion,nashid2023assertion} to TOGA \citep{dinella2022toga}; FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} and \citet{foster2025mutation} demonstrated structured fault signals.
These approaches treat traces as monolithic inputs; none isolate individual components or compare against rule-based baselines.

\paragraph{Fault Localization.}
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL) ranks program elements by suspiciousness from test spectra; classic metrics (Ochiai \citep{abreu2007accuracy}, Tarantula \citep{jones2002visualization}, DStar \citep{wong2014dstar}) and recent LLM-based approaches \citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl,widyasari2024llm4fl,mukherjee2025llmfl} share our core insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal.
Verdict prediction is a prerequisite to FL: one must determine \emph{whether} a fault exists before localizing \emph{where}.
Our approach and SBFL operate at different granularities (test-level vs.\ statement-level) but exploit the same signal type.

\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}
TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction for debugging; RepairAgent \citep{bouzenia2025repairagent} and Agentless \citep{xia2024agentless} incorporate execution feedback in repair workflows.
\citet{haque2025traces} found raw traces provide limited repair benefit, supporting our compression finding.
SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench} provides a realistic benchmark for agents reasoning about test execution.
Our approximate information density decomposition (gradient dilution ${\sim}$24\% vs.\ information overload ${\sim}$76\%) provides the first quantitative framework for \emph{why} compression helps, complementing these methods' focus on \emph{how} to compress.

\paragraph{Calibration and Defect Prediction.}
Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,spiess2025calibration}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; our ECE ${<}$ 0.007 suggests compact inputs improve calibration.
Just-in-time defect prediction progressed from feature engineering \citep{kamei2013large} through deep learning \citep{hoang2019deepjit} to simpler-but-effective approaches \citep{pornprasit2021jitline}; these methods share our fault detection motivation but operate on code change features rather than execution traces.

\paragraph{Training Efficiency and Data Selection.}
Curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, dataset cartography via training dynamics \citep{swayamdipta2020cartography}, and data selection methods \citep{sachdeva2024dataefficient,xie2023doremi} show that data quality and ordering improve convergence, consistent with our finding that compact exceptions enable rapid convergence while verbose traces trap the model in oscillation.

\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction across four models (1.5B--13B, three architecture families).
Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four models (${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds; 3-seed mean 96.58\% due to format collapse on one seed), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows 9.16pp scale sensitivity (67.3--76.5\%).
Adding more trace information provides no additional benefit: training dynamics show \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence.
The gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) on Qwen-7B (3 seeds).
A format-marker ablation shows ${\sim}$91\% of the exception signal is semantic rather than format-driven, and cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench confirms generalization (\texttt{exception\_only}: 100\%, $N{=}426$).

The broader implication is that verdict prediction is not an information-starved task that benefits from richer context.
It is a fault detection task where the runtime has already surfaced the critical diagnostic signal; the model's role is to interpret whether that signal indicates a terminal fault (as the SFT advantage over regex on caught-exception cases confirms).
This reframing suggests a design principle for trace-augmented systems: extract the highest-specificity diagnostic signal (median 150 tokens) and discard everything else.
Our findings are established on LLM-generated Python code with exception-dominated error distributions; whether they hold for other languages, larger real-world codebases, production fault distributions with a higher proportion of silent logic errors (where no exception is raised), or tasks beyond verdict prediction remains an open question.

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
Yet feeding thousands of trace lines to a model can be no better than feeding none: the diagnostic signal drowns in routine execution steps.
\emph{Which trace components actually carry the signal that matters?}

Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
\emph{Verdict prediction}, classifying whether a test passes or fails, is fundamentally different: it is fault detection, not generation.
The model need not simulate execution; it need only determine whether something went wrong.
This distinction suggests that a small, fault-specific trace component may suffice.

We test this hypothesis through the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.
The results are counterintuitive: complete traces (82--88\%) underperform a single compact component (${\geq}$99\%) despite containing strictly more information, because verbose content drowns the diagnostic signal.

\textbf{Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% verdict accuracy on three of four models (${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 seeds for the fourth; one seed reaches 100\%).}
DeepSeek-6.7B is the exception: its 3-seed mean is 96.58\% ($\pm$4.76pp) due to one seed exhibiting format collapse (fail recall = 70.5\%), though even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
This near-perfect accuracy holds from 1.5B to 13B parameters, while the code-only baseline (\texttt{no\_trace}) varies from 67.3\% to 76.5\% with strong scale dependence.
Training dynamics expose the mechanism (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}): \texttt{exception\_only} converges to 99.33\% within 50 training steps and saturates at 99.83\% by step 150, while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates between 82\% and 89\% across the entire training without stable convergence, consistent with overfitting to spurious patterns in verbose content.

Adding trace information beyond exceptions provides no benefit and can degrade performance: VOTA (3-seed mean 99.05\%) underperforms \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) on Qwen-7B, with the gap reaching 14.96pp on DeepSeek due to tokenizer-driven truncation.
The performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%).
A tail-truncation budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens, with \texttt{tail\_2048} recovering 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy.
Even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), \texttt{exception\_only} maintains 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exception events are the minimal sufficient signal for verdict prediction on LLM-generated code}: ${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four models, ${\geq}$99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds (1.5B--13B, three families), with ${\sim}$91\% of the signal being semantic rather than format-driven (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}). Cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) yields 100\% (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Training dynamics reveal the convergence mechanism}: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates (82--89\%) without stable convergence, consistent with overfitting to verbose content. SFT on exception events closes a 6--49pp zero-shot gap across all four models (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
\item \textbf{Richer traces provide no additional benefit}: We approximately decompose the performance gap into gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%) and information overload (${\sim}$76\%), based on Qwen-7B (3 seeds). A budget sweep across four models reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens, with \texttt{tail\_2048} recovering 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only} (\S\ref{sec:density}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy (observed on Qwen-7B)}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) individually achieve ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 (loop compression) reaches 86.1\%, still +10.9pp over no trace. Cross-model \texttt{exception\_only} consistency suggests this hierarchy may generalize, though direct verification on other models remains future work (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}
